title: NetworkDB does not always reliably converge
body:
### Description

In our setups, we keep having issues around Docker DNS resolution around times where we either:

1. restart Docker nodes in quick succession
2. update Docker nodes (and therefore restart them in quick succession)
3. have network issues

For a second we thought that the MTU settings for the networking controlplane might be the issue, but the issue seems to have happened even on an MTU that fits our setup (we used 1350 instead of the default 1500).

It seems that during these times, the gossip network of networkdb does not get synched up properly. We debugged this with the built in debugging tooling of libnetwork (which is really helpful btw) and found that there exists no mechanism in dockerd that concerns itself with resynching the `endpoint_table` of networkdb (or `overlay_peer_table` for that matter but that does not seem to be that much of a problem). We double checked this by going through the code of libnetwork/agent.go:

The only places that update anything in networkdb are calls to `addServiceInfoToCluster` (CreateEntry), `addDriverInfoToCluster` (CreateEntry), `deleteDriverInfoFromCluster` (DeleteEntry), `deleteServiceInfoFromCluster` (DeleteEntry). `disableServiceInNetworkDB` (UpdateEntry).

While we might have missed things, here comes our proposal: There should be a (opt-in) docker daemon config option that enables a background job in the docker daemon that on a schedule resyncs all the DNS entries to networkdb. Design wise I have not thought about it a lot, but I imagine that this should be fine to run on a schedule of maybe 1-5 minutes in most clusters. This way, whenever a DNS entry is out of sync things should fix themselves in a somewhat acceptable schedule.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body: NetworkDB not converging in a reasonable amount of time is a bug. It does look like `bulkSync` is intended to be that resynching mechanism you suggest, though apparently it is not working properly. To a first approximation, NetworkDB is a distributed KV store with multiple "keyspaces" (called networks) where each node in the cluster gets to pick and choose which keyspaces to participate in. A node only holds the state for the keyspaces it participates in, and therefore can only receive state updates from other nodes also participating. ~I suspect (from a cursory reading of a small slice of the networkdb package source) that there is a design flaw in how this is implemented: the mapping of nodes to networks is only updated with broadcasts, with no mechanism for recovering from a missed broadcast. That mapping probably has to be reliably distributed—like the KV pairs themselves are—to all nodes in the cluster for bulk sync to reliably converge in imperfect conditions.~

comments.author: participant2
comments.body: I think there's merit to the "system tables" idea I sketched out in https://github.com/moby/moby/issues/47728#issuecomment-2073364693. NetworkDB has already solved the challenges you mention for keeping the table entries themselves within a keyspace up to date. And NetworkDB has a reliable list of all nodes participating in the cluster thanks to the memberlist module. If we had tables where all records are implicitly part of a system keyspace which all nodes in the cluster participate in, the same reliable gossip logic could be used for NetworkDB bookkeeping as is used to synchronize user tables. With such infrastructure in place, NetworkDB could simply use a system table to distribute the node-network mappings reliably to the whole cluster.

The metadata _which is currently only propagated using broadcasts_ would instead be propagated through a new system table. The system tables would be reserved for internal NetworkDB bookkeeping only -- like PostgreSQL's system catalogues.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
> Currently trying to find what you mean by `the per-network tables`. Can you point me to the code that handles this case already?

The code which handles per-network tables is the meat of NetworkDB. For example, `endpoint_table` is a per-network table. Though to reduce confusion I am going to refer to them as "user tables" from now on. (Remember, in NetworkDB parlance, a "network" is really a namespace for table entries; one of the database dimensions.) So to answer your question, the entrypoints for the code which handles the "per-network" user tables are the exported NetworkDB methods for tables and entries: `CreateEntry`, `DeleteEntry`, `UpdateEntry`, `DeleteEntry`, `GetTableByNetwork`, `WalkTable`, `Watch`.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body: I think I may have been wrong in my earlier diagnosis. The NetworkDB code [is (ostensibly) reliably distributing the mapping of nodes to networks](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/1dd102e9b64e56debec06579fa08210c18f0f37a/libnetwork/networkdb/delegate.go#L412-L494) through memberlist's gossip layer TCP push/pull mechanism in addition to unreliable broadcasts. With each push/pull gossiping the complete state of the mapping, and the push/pull interval left at the 30-second default, the mapping should be expected to converge across all nodes within a few minutes. The root cause may be a much more subtle bug, which on the one hand means more debugging is required to identify the root cause, but on the other hand gives me hope that it might be fixable without any protocol-level changes!

comments.author: participant4
comments.body:
As far as I understand, this will only help for the cases where the `endpoint` table of the networkdb is corrupt. If the `overlay_peer` table is corrupt - either no entry for the endpoint IP or an incorrect TunnelEndpointIp value, a different DNS server won't help. In fact, in these cases not even using the IP address instead of the DNS name will help, because the packages are not being routed to the correct node.

<strike>I've created a tool that simply deletes incorrect entries from the networkdb: https://github.com/sovarto/swarm-network-fixer (run as service, mode global, using host network and map 3175 to host and /var/run/docker.sock into the service)
Unfortunately, this doesn't seem to be enough.</strike> (Don't use, fixing the entries of networkDB has no effect at all)

I think that there are multiple layers of issues to these networking problems:
1. Incorrect or missing DNS entries in `endpoint` table. **Consequence**: Resolution of service name to IP address fails or results in an incorrect address
2. Incorrect or missing routing info in `overlay_peer` table. **Consequence**: Packages get routed to a node that doesn't actually run the container with the given IP address
3. Broken VXLAN setup on some nodes (???), triggered by errors in the networkdb (???). **Consequence**: Packages have the correct target IP and get routed to the correct node, but are not reaching the container. Verified via tcpdump: Packages are visible on the correct node on its physical network interface, but they aren't visible in the VXLAN interface that belongs to the overlay network.

1 and 2 I can fix via docker restart. But 3, I can only "fix" by creating a completely new overlay network and moving all services to the new one. Update: 3 can actually be fixed by manually fixing vxlan and fdb entries, see gist I linked in a later comment.

comments.body:
For some added context and for those experiencing this issue and looking for a solution, here's what worked for me.

The error when trying to update an affected service:
```sh
$ docker service update 012j1cjl2kjc
network sandbox join failed: subnet sandbox join failed for "10.0.5.0/24": error creating vxlan interface: file exists
```
The solution without the need to restart: (based on [this comment](https://github.com/moby/libnetwork/issues/562#issuecomment-1155015141))
```sh
$ ip -d link show | grep vx # find the problem
538009: vx-001005-lhn5p: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST> mtu 1450 qdisc noop state DOWN mode DEFAULT group default
    vxlan id 4101 srcport 0 0 dstport 4789 proxy l2miss l3miss ttl auto ageing 300 udpcsum noudp6zerocsumtx noudp6zerocsumrx addrgenmode eui64 numtxqueues 1 numrxqueues 1 gso_max_size 65536 gso_max_segs 65535 tso_max_size 65536 tso_max_segs 65535 gro_max_size 65536 gso_ipv4_max_size 65536 gro_ipv4_max_size 65536

$ docker network ls | grep -E "lhn5p" # show the associated overlay network
lhn5pw0ttydq   mynetwork_default          overlay   swarm

$ sudo ip link delete vx-001005-lhn5p # delete it: problem solved!
```
Hopefully there will be a structural solution soon!

comments.body:
@participant7 Hi! You've come to the right place.

When you restart your Swarm, do you perform a rolling restart or do you shut down all nodes before starting them back up? Are you just stopping and restarting the dockerd service, or performing a full reboot of the host?

When you say that the container "randomly" loses connectivity to the other container, could you elaborate? How does that relate to the cluster restarts? Are the host-0 and host-1 containers able to communicate at first after the cluster restarts, then breaks some time after? Is it initially broken then heals?

The logs and packet captures you have provided are pretty informative, but don't show the whole picture. It would help me debug if you could provide the following from each affected host:
1. The service table dump for the affected overlay network. Note that you need to specify the full-length network ID on the command line for the diagnostic tool to work properly. You can find that using the `docker network ls --no-trunc` command.
2. A dump of the overlay table on the affected nodes: `docker run --net host dockereng/network-diagnostic:onlyclient -port 2000 -v -net $NETWORK_ID -t overlay 2>&1`
3. Dumps of the forwarding databases for the VXLAN network links on the nodes: `bridge fdb show dev vxlan0` inside the correct namespace.
4. The IP addresses assigned to the affected containers on the overlay network. I can work with either the output of the `ip a` command from inside the containers, or `docker container inspect` output.

Feel free to reach out to me on the [Docker Community Slack](http://dockr.ly/comm-slack) workspace if you need any assistance gathering the debugging info above. I go by the same username there.

comments.body:
It looks to me that three distinct types of failure mode are being discussed in this issue's comments:

1. NetworkDB state gets corrupted in some way. (This issue)
2. NetworkDB state is correct, but the overlay network's data plane (VXLAN FDB, etc.) gets out of sync with what NetworkDB says. Let's continue debugging that failure mode over in #49908
3. `error creating vxlan interface: file exists`. That is being discussed in #49555

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
@participant2 i see you have been busy :)

So essentially you have found a bug in the behaviour for propagation of entries in NetworkDB that happens around dying/dead nodes?

comments.author: participant2
comments.body: Not quite; simply having a container flapping, if it's the only one on the node attached to the network, is sufficient to trigger the bug. It's the sequence of events of leaving a network, rejoining, and creating an entry that is the problem. If some other node receives the events in the order CREATE, LeaveNetwork, JoinNetwork, it will mark the entry as deleted and ignore any other copies of the CREATE event (e.g. through bulk syncs) which say otherwise. Once in that state, the node will only converge after one of two things happen. The owning node could update the entry, superseding the bugged marked-as-deleted entry. Or the marked-as-deleted entry gets garbage collected after 30 minutes, allowing the node to accept the non-deleted entry from the next bulk sync. There have been reports that the cluster does self-heal after around 30 minutes; this is why.
